procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated September 22, 1965 of the Patna High Court in Government Appeal No. 40 of 1962 with Cr. Revision No. 122 of 1963.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State of Bihar filed an appeal and a revision petition for enhancement of the sentence. The High Court allowed the appeal and revision petition in part. It convicted Sheonath, Matukdeo and Sarjoo under sec. 395 and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years each, enhanced the sentences already imposed on them under sec. 353 by adding a sentence of two years rigorous imprisonment against each of them and directed that the substantive sentences of imprisonment would run concurrently. It convicted Satnarayan, Billat and Gullat of offences under sec. 395 and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year each, enhanced the sentences imposed upon them under sec. 153/149 by adding sentences of one years rigorous imprisonment against each of them and directed that the substantive sentences of imprisonment would run concurrently. It acquitted Bishwanath of all the charges.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Sheonath, Matukdeo, Sarjoo, Satnarayan, Billat and Gullat filed an appeal after obtaining special leave from the Supreme Court.

decision.appeal_result: the appeal is allowed in part.
decision.conviction_status: The convictions of the appellants by the courts below including their convictions by the High Court under sec. 395 are affirmed.
decision.sentence_status: The sentences under sec. 395 and the enhanced sentences in respect of other offences imposed on the appellants by the High Court are reduced to the period of imprisonment already undergone by them. The sentences imposed on the appellants by the 3rd Assistant Sessions Judge, Patna, are maintained.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power of inspection, seizure and search under s. 17 of the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1947 can be exercised only in a place of business declared by the dealer under the Act and the Rules.

facts: A Superintendent of Commercial Taxes found a dealer keeping a duplicate set of accounts at a secret location (gaddi).
This secret location was not declared by the dealer as a place of business in their registration application under the Bihar Sales Tax Act.
The Superintendent, exercising powers under Section 17 of the Act, searched this location and seized the account books.

law.description: Grants the tax authorities the power to inspect, search, and seize accounts and documents at any "place of business" of a dealer.
Defines a "place of business" as "any place where a dealer sells goods or keeps accounts of sales."

application: The Court first looked at the legal definition of a "place of business" under Rule 2(l).

It found that since the dealer kept accounts of sales at the secret gaddi, that location factually met the legal definition of a "place of business," regardless of whether it had been officially declared.
The Court reasoned that while the Act requires a dealer to declare all places of business, it does not state that an undeclared location is immune from search.
To rule otherwise would allow a dealer to evade the law simply by failing to declare a location where they conduct business or keep records.

The Court further noted that the search power under Section 17 also applies to unregistered dealers, who by definition have not declared any place of business. This shows the power is not dependent on a prior declaration by the dealer.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the power of inspection, search, and seizure under Section 17 is not limited to a place of business officially declared by a dealer. The power can be exercised in respect of any and every location that fits the legal definition of a "place of business," which includes any place where a dealer keeps accounts of sales.

issue.issue_text: Whether the search and seizure were illegal due to non-compliance with s. 165(4) read with s. 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code, on the grounds that the search was made in the course of an investigation of a cognizable offence.

facts: An officer, Sharma, conducted an inspection, search, and seizure of account books.
The appellant argued that this action was part of an investigation into a cognizable offense.
Sharma stated he was not authorized to investigate an offense.
Sharma's authority was delegated to him under s. 17 of the Bihar Sales Tax Act, which grants powers of inspection, search, and seizure.
law: The provisions of s. 165(4) read with s. 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code apply to searches conducted during the investigation of a cognizable offense.
application: The Supreme Court was not satisfied that Sharma conducted the search and seizure in the course of investigating a cognizable offense.
The Court found that Sharma was exercising the specific powers of inspection, search, and seizure granted to him under s. 17 of the Bihar Sales Tax Act.

Since Sharma was not investigating or dealing with an offense, but rather acting under the authority of the Sales Tax Act, the procedural requirements of the Criminal Procedure Code were not applicable.
Therefore, Sharma was not required to comply with the provisions of s. 165(4) and s. 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
reasoning.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument, concluding that the search and seizure were not illegal because the officer was acting under the powers of the Bihar Sales Tax Act (s. 17), not investigating a cognizable offense. Consequently, the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code did not apply.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sentences imposed on the appellants should be mitigated.

facts: The lower courts had described the offense of dacoity as "a technical one."
The appellants did not cause any physical harm to any member of the raiding party.
The appellants had already served about a month in prison.
application: Considering the technical nature of the offense, the lack of violence, and the time already served, the Court determined that a reduced sentence would be appropriate.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the "ends of justice" would be met by reducing the sentences imposed by the High Court to the period of imprisonment the appellants had already undergone.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the search and seizure were illegal due to non-compliance with s. 165(4) read with s. 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code, on the grounds that the search was made in the course of an investigation of a cognizable offence.
appellant_arguments: The search and seizure were conducted in the course of an investigation of a cognizable offense (maintaining incorrect accounts).
Therefore, the search should have complied with the procedural requirements of s. 165(4) and s. 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The failure to comply with these provisions made the search and seizure illegal.
respondent_arguments: The Superintendent (Sharma) was not investigating a cognizable offense; he was only exercising powers delegated to him under s. 17 of the Sales Tax Act.
Sharma was not authorized by the Commissioner under s. 27 to investigate an offense.
As he was not investigating an offense, the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code were not attracted and he was not required to comply with them.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sentences imposed on the appellants should be mitigated.
appellant_arguments: The offense of dacoity was a 'technical' one.
No physical hurt was caused to any member of the raiding party during the incident.
respondent_arguments: The provided text does not contain the respondent's arguments against the mitigation of the sentence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power of inspection, search, and seizure under Section 17 of the Bihar Sales Tax Act is not limited to a place of business officially declared by a dealer in an application for registration. This power can be exercised in respect of any location that qualifies as a "place of business," which includes any place where a dealer keeps accounts of sales. A search and seizure conducted solely under the authority of Section 17 of the Act is not an investigation of a cognizable offense, and therefore, the procedural requirements of Sections 165(4) and 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code do not apply.
obiter: The court observed that the offense of dacoity was a technical one and that the appellants did not cause hurt to any member of the raiding party, which were factors considered in the mitigation of the sentence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Superintendent of Commercial Taxes was not investigating a cognizable offense but was lawfully exercising the specific powers of inspection, search, and seizure delegated to him under s. 17 of the Bihar Sales Tax Act. Consequently, the procedural requirements of the Criminal Procedure Code were not applicable to his actions, rendering the search and seizure legal.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a test to determine the applicable legal regime by distinguishing between the powers exercised under a specific civil statute (the Bihar Sales Tax Act) and the powers exercised during the investigation of a cognizable offense under the general criminal law (the Criminal Procedure Code). The character of the officer's action—whether it was a statutory inspection or a criminal investigation—determined which set of procedural rules applied.
why_appellant_lost: The court was not satisfied that the tax officer (Sharma) made the search and seizure in the course of an investigation of a cognizable offense.
The officer was not authorized by the Commissioner under s. 27 of the Sales Tax Act to investigate an offense; only the powers under s. 17 had been delegated to him.

Because the officer was exercising powers under s. 17 of the Sales Tax Act and was not investigating or dealing with an offense, the procedural requirements of s. 165(4) read with s. 103 of the Criminal Procedure Code were not attracted.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the tax officer was only exercising the powers delegated to him under s. 17 of the Bihar Sales Tax Act.
The court found that the officer was not investigating or dealing with an offense, which meant the procedural requirements of the Criminal Procedure Code did not apply to his actions.
policy_considerations: In mitigating the sentence, the court considered that the offense of dacoity was a 'technical one' under the circumstances.
The court noted as a mitigating factor that the appellants did not cause hurt to any member of the raiding party.
The court concluded that considering the nature of the offense and the time already served, 'the ends of justice will be met' by reducing the sentences imposed by the High Court.
